item.title: Subcycle videography of Landau–Zener–Majorana transitions in graphene
item.dc:creator: V. Eggers
G. Inzani
M. Meierhofer
L. Münster
J. Helml
R. Wallauer
S. Zajusch
S. Ito
item.description:
Authors: V. Eggers, G. Inzani, M. Meierhofer, L. Münster, J. Helml, R. Wallauer, S. Zajusch, S. Ito, et al.
Journal: Nature
Abstract: Abstract Strong light fields have unlocked entirely new possibilities to tailor coherent electron trajectories, engineer band structures and shape emergent phases of matter all-optically 1–9 . Unravelling the underlying quantum mechanisms requires a visualization of the lightwave-driven electron motion 10,11 directly in the band structure. Although photoelectron momentum microscopy has imaged photoexcited electrons averaged over many cycles of light 12–19 , subcycle band-structure videography has been limited to small electron momenta 8,20 . Yet, lightwave-driven elementary processes in quantum materials often occur throughout momentum space. Here we introduce attosecond-precision, subcycle band-structure videography covering the entire first Brillouin zone and visualize one of the most fundamental but elusive strong-field processes: non-adiabatic Landau–Zener–Majorana tunnelling. The interplay of strong-field-driven acceleration within the Dirac-like band structure of graphene and periodic Landau–Zener–Majorana interband tunnelling manifests in a coherent subcycle displacement and distortion of the carrier distribution at the Brillouin zone edge. The extremely non-thermal electron distributions also allow us to disentangle competing scattering processes and assess their impact on coherent electronic control. Our panoramic view of field-driven electron motion enables a new quality of microscopic understanding of strong-field control of quantum materials.

item.title: Perinatal elimination of genetically aberrant human cortical neurons
item.dc:creator: Diane D. Shao
Yifan Zhao
Joseph Brew
Yahia Adla
Urmi Ghosh
Vinayak V. Viswanadham
Lovelace J. Luquette
Sijing Zhao
item.description:
Authors: Diane D. Shao, Yifan Zhao, Joseph Brew, Yahia Adla, Urmi Ghosh, Vinayak V. Viswanadham, Lovelace J. Luquette, Sijing Zhao, et al.
Journal: Nature
Abstract: Abstract Human neurons are postmitotic and long-lived, requiring precise genomic regulation. Normal neuronal function is highly dosage-sensitive, with copy number variants (CNVs) and heterozygous point mutations associated with a host of neurodevelopmental and neuropsychiatric conditions 1–4 . Here we investigated somatic CNVs arising in single neurons to understand the dynamic processes that shape the normal neuronal genetic landscape. Altogether, we sequenced 2,357 single neurons from human postmortem brain from fetal to postnatal life. Two single-cell whole-genome sequencing approaches—Tn5-transposase-based amplification (1,526 neurons, 16 individuals) and primary template amplification 5 (831 neurons, 12 individuals)—showed that an average of 25.9% [12.7–46%] of prenatal cortical neurons have highly aberrant genomes, that is, widespread CNVs involving multiple chromosomes. This proportion reduced by about 4.5-fold after birth across the two single-cell whole-genome sequencing approaches (Fisher meta-analysis P = 3.5 × 10 − 6 ). Neurons with widespread CNVs were mainly eliminated perinatally, timed roughly parallel to periods of programmed cell death 6 , whereas neurons with smaller CNV burdens declined slowly in frequency with postnatal age. CNVs in surviving neurons were depleted for dosage-sensitive genes and genes involved in neurodevelopmental disorders (hypergeometric test P < 0.05), suggesting selective elimination of neurons with these CNVs. Analysis of 44,861 nuclei with single-nucleus assay for transposase-accessible chromatin (snATAC) and single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq) showed that neurons with high CNV burdens exhibited abnormal synaptic gene expression, suggesting that abnormal synaptic gene regulation contributes to neuronal elimination. Elimination of defective neuronal genomes might represent an important developmental genome quality-control process that may be vulnerable in neurodevelopmental disease, and suggests purifying selection during human neurodevelopment.

item.title: Spatial and sectoral water demand assessment for the African continent
item.dc:creator: Davy Vanham
Dahami Gunathilake
Bhawani Gunasekara
Seifu Tilahun
Youssef Brouziyne
Fasikaw A. Zimale
Monika Rawat
Raphael Vanham
item.description:
Authors: Davy Vanham, Dahami Gunathilake, Bhawani Gunasekara, Seifu Tilahun, Youssef Brouziyne, Fasikaw A. Zimale, Monika Rawat, Raphael Vanham, et al.
Journal: Nature
Abstract: Abstract Water demand is the volume of water required by a sector to satisfy its needs 1,2 . Across Africa, these demands are frequently unmet 3 , yet their spatial and sectoral distribution remains incompletely characterized, limiting informed water-management decisions 4 . Here, we provide an Africa-wide estimate of water demand for 2020 across six sectors and multiple subsectors at high spatial resolution. Because the analysis integrates heterogeneous datasets and modelling assumptions, the resulting values should be interpreted as harmonized estimates rather than direct observations of realized water use. We estimate total annual water demand at 347 km 3 , comprising 60 km 3 (17%) for municipalities (57–64 km 3 , with ±20% key parameters variations), 225 km 3 (65%) for irrigation (214–233 km 3 , 95% confidence interval, with ±20% variations in irrigation efficiency), 11 km 3 (3%) for livestock, 15 km 3 (4%) for manufacturing, 33 km 3 (10%) for electricity including hydropower and 3 km 3 (1%) for mining (3–4 km 3 , with annual production variations). Estimated demand increased by 26% between 2010 and 2020. The dominant water-demand sector varies across regions and river basins, broadly reflecting established geographical and socioeconomic patterns. In parts of northern and southern Africa, estimated demand exceeds water availability, although results depend on assumptions regarding environmental-flow protection 5 . Elsewhere, water availability exceeds aggregate demand despite limited access to piped drinking water, indicating that physical availability alone does not determine water security. Our analysis therefore provides a spatially and sectorally resolved baseline for identifying water-demand pressures and access constraints rather than establishing a new causal mechanism of water insecurity. Local estimates should be interpreted cautiously given uncertainties in the underlying datasets.

item.title: Eukaryotes’ closest relatives are internally simple syntrophic peptidotrophic archaea
item.dc:creator: Hiroyuki Imachi
Masaru K. Nobu
Shun’ichi Ishii
Hiroki Hashiguchi
Yuga Hirakata
Naoki Hosogi
Tetsuro Ikuta
Yuta Isaji
item.description:
Authors: Hiroyuki Imachi, Masaru K. Nobu, Shun’ichi Ishii, Hiroki Hashiguchi, Yuga Hirakata, Naoki Hosogi, Tetsuro Ikuta, Yuta Isaji, et al.
Journal: Nature
Abstract: Abstract Eukaryotes are theorized to have an origin associated with the archaeal phylum Promethearchaeota (formerly Asgard archaea) 1–3 . The first cultured representatives revealed valuable insights 4,5 but are still distantly related to eukaryotes, leaving many unknowns regarding eukaryogenesis. Here we report the isolation of two strains, HC1 and SC1, that belong to the archaeal lineage that branches closest to eukaryotes (Heimdallarchaeia); 6–8 these isolates are members of a pure co-culture and a tri-culture with methanogenic partners. Both are obligately anaerobic, syntrophic, peptide-degrading and mesophilic archaea that produce protrusions and vesicles but lack persistent internal membrane structures, like Promethearchaeales 4,5 . All Promethearchaeota isolates demonstrate behaviour focused on cell construction and membrane structures rather than division, in contrast to typical prokaryotes 9 . Strain HC1 possesses genes associated with aerobic lifestyles (such as cytochrome c oxidase (Cox)) but co-cultures cannot grow under (micro)oxic conditions. Meanwhile, the strain demonstrates growth under microoxic conditions when in the presence of aerobes, suggesting that Cox supports oxygen detoxification rather than respiration. Comparative genomics provides evidence that, like HC1, Cox-possessing Heimdallarchaeia studied to date probably do not respire oxygen. The wide conservation of anaerobiosis, cell structure without persistent intracellular membranes and membrane protrusions across Promethearchaeota suggest that the archaeal ancestor of eukaryotes may have had such physiological features. In this cultivation-informed scenario for eukaryogenesis, the archaea–eukaryote transition would involve a steep transition in cell structure and physiological shift from anaerobiosis to (facultative) aerobiosis 10 , with early interactions between the archaeal host and mitochondrial ancestor probably occurring under low-oxygen conditions and at least partially mediated by oxygen detoxification.

item.title: SWI/SNF complexes shape 3D chromatin architecture through CTCF and cohesin
item.dc:creator: Sonia Debek
Cem Meydan
Christopher R. Chin
Jiali Yu
Ceyda Durmaz
Ioanna Tsialta
Benedikt Pelzer
Constance Maurer
item.description:
Authors: Sonia Debek, Cem Meydan, Christopher R. Chin, Jiali Yu, Ceyda Durmaz, Ioanna Tsialta, Benedikt Pelzer, Constance Maurer, et al.
Journal: Nature
Abstract: Abstract The BAF (also known as mammalian SWI/SNF) chromatin remodelling complexes are essential regulators of nucleosome positioning and transcription factor binding 1,2 . Loss-of-function (LOF) mutations in genes encoding components of the BAF complexes are among the most frequent across cancer types 3 . However, a unifying mechanism that explains their widespread disruption remains unclear. Here we disrupted BAF function through pharmacological inhibition and ARID1A deletion across various mammalian cell types and tissues and observed a conserved chromatin response: increased accessibility at CTCF-binding sites. ARID1A LOF alone was sufficient to drive these changes, which demonstrates that canonical BAF (cBAF) disruption is the key driver of CTCF gain. Genomic profiling showed increased CTCF and SMC3 occupancy, which reveals an antagonistic relationship between cBAF and CTCF–cohesin complexes. Furthermore, cBAF loss restructured 3D genome organization, which led to a strengthening of topologically associating domain boundaries and subdivision of large domains into smaller insulated structures. Long-range enhancer–promoter loops were replaced by shorter, promoter-proximal loops anchored at CTCF-enriched sites. To determine how CTCF function is enabled following cBAF loss, we profiled CTCF-interacting cofactors and found that CTCF binds directly to fully assembled PBAF. After cBAF depletion, PBAF was recruited to sites of increased CTCF occupancy, which demonstrates that there is an antagonistic switch between SWI/SNF subcomplexes. In vivo, conditional Arid1a deletion in primary mouse cells resulted in the expansion of a highly proliferative population marked by elevated accessibility at CTCF sites. This phenotype was fully reversed by either Ctcf or Pbrm1 deletion, which establishes that cBAF and the activity of CTCF and PBAF have contrasting roles.

item.title: Delayed electron–hole recombination in a pseudo-direct semiconductor
item.dc:creator: Marcello Righetto
Debalina Banerjee
Zhenglin Jia
Joshua R. S. Lilly
Vincent J. -Y. Lim
Snigdha Lal
Siyu Yan
Jae Eun Lee
item.description:
Authors: Marcello Righetto, Debalina Banerjee, Zhenglin Jia, Joshua R. S. Lilly, Vincent J. -Y. Lim, Snigdha Lal, Siyu Yan, Jae Eun Lee, et al.
Journal: Nature
Abstract: Abstract Kirchhoff demonstrated the reciprocity between absorptivity and emissivity for blackbody radiation in 1860 (ref. 1 ), thereby establishing the general principle that a good absorber must also be a good emitter. This principle underpins the generalized Planck’s law 2 and, when applied to semiconductors—in the form of the van Roosbroeck–Shockley equation 3 —results in substantial limitations to solar energy conversion. Here we demonstrate how this reciprocity can be circumvented in semiconductors, such as bismuth sulfide, showing a pseudo-direct bandgap character—that is, featuring a lower-energy indirect transition paired with a direct transition placed a few k B T above. After determining the pseudo-direct bandgap nature of bismuth sulfide, we reveal how this feature substantially retards bimolecular electron–hole recombination in this material with respect to classic direct semiconductors 4 . The resulting combination of a high absorption coefficient and delayed recombination offers the unprecedented possibility of overcoming limitations associated with Planck’s law, with far-reaching potential for solar energy conversion.

item.title: Tumour assembloids recapitulate tumour–CAF–T cell crosstalk in renal cancer
item.dc:creator: Eunjee Kim
Minyong Kang
Jang Hee Han
Juhee Lee
Yunhee Kim
Chang Wook Jeong
HyeSun Lee
Hyun Je Kim
item.description:
Authors: Eunjee Kim, Minyong Kang, Jang Hee Han, Juhee Lee, Yunhee Kim, Chang Wook Jeong, HyeSun Lee, Hyun Je Kim, et al.
Journal: Nature
Abstract: Abstract Dynamic interactions between tumours and their microenvironment are crucial for cancer progression and therapeutic outcomes 1,2 . However, our understanding of these relationships remains limited by the constrained capacity of current human model systems to manipulate diverse cellular components and to interrogate complex tumour–stroma crosstalk. Here we generated combinatorial, mix-and-match tumour assembloids by conditionally reconstituting multiple components of human renal cell carcinoma, including cancer cells, cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) and tumour-infiltrating immune cells. Using genetically engineered renal cell carcinoma assembloids with humanized mouse models, we uncovered mechanisms by which CAFs coordinate interactions between tumour cells and CD8 + T cells to maintain non-cell-autonomous CD8 + T cell stemness and drive responsiveness to anti-PD-1 therapy. These interactions operate through a tumour–CAF–T cell signalling axis in which tumour-derived WNT induces CAF expression of activin A, which enhances CD8 + T cell stemness and sensitivity to PD-1 blockade. In non-responders, we also identified a subset of WNT-unresponsive CAFs that do not produce activin A, which leads to impaired CD8 + T cell stemness and resistance to therapy. Together, these findings establish a tumour–CAF–T cell axis as a key determinant of heterogeneous responses to immune checkpoint inhibitors. Moreover, tumour assembloids provide a versatile platform for mechanistic dissection of the tumour microenvironment and evaluation of personalized immunotherapy strategies.

item.title: A single-molecule spin–photon interface
item.dc:creator: Simon Roggors
Thomas Unden
Anna Aubele
Paul Mentzel
Gregor Bayer
Alon Salhov
Jochen Scharpf
Martin B. Plenio
item.description:
Authors: Simon Roggors, Thomas Unden, Anna Aubele, Paul Mentzel, Gregor Bayer, Alon Salhov, Jochen Scharpf, Martin B. Plenio, et al.
Journal: Nature; Volume: 658; Issue: 8138; Pages: 1153-1159
Abstract: Abstract Optical interfaces that connect long-lived spin qubits to photons are a central requirement for quantum networking and distributed quantum information processing. At present, solid-state atomic defects are leading candidates because of their inherent spin and optical coherence 1,2 . Building on these advancements, synthetically tailored molecular systems represent a fundamental change in the field, using precise atomic control and consistent bottom-up assembly 3,4 . However, a molecular platform that concurrently satisfies the demands of a robust spin–photon interface—namely, the combination of bright fluorescence, high spectral stability and long ground-state spin lifetimes—has yet to be realized at the single-molecule level. Here we show that a triplet ground-state carbene molecule, embedded within a structurally matched host crystal, functions as a robust spin–photon interface with single-molecule addressability. The system exhibits narrow ZPLs, spectral stability over more than an hour, spin-selective optical transitions and single-molecule optically detected magnetic resonance. Coherent control yields millisecond-scale dynamical-decoupling coherence and tens-of-milliseconds spin relaxation at a temperature of 4.5 K. These results establish molecular qubits as a viable platform for single-emitter quantum optics 5,6 while preserving the advantages of bottom-up chemical design 7 and processable materials 8–10 .

item.title: MCT1-dependent mitochondrial lactate import sustains cardiac metabolism
item.dc:creator: Ahmad A. Cluntun
Joseph R. Visker
Jesse N. Velasco-Silva
James Carrington
Luis Cedeño-Rosario
Giulia C. Napoli
Ji Eon Kim
Thirupura S. Shankar
item.description:
Authors: Ahmad A. Cluntun, Joseph R. Visker, Jesse N. Velasco-Silva, James Carrington, Luis Cedeño-Rosario, Giulia C. Napoli, Ji Eon Kim, Thirupura S. Shankar, et al.
Journal: Nature
Abstract: Abstract The heart possesses a dynamic capacity to oxidize a variety of fuels, including glucose and lactate, to meet its energetic demands under diverse dietary, exertion and injury stressors 1 . Oxidation of carbohydrate substrates is thought to converge on the cytosolic generation of pyruvate, which is transported by the mitochondrial pyruvate carrier (MPC) for entry into the tricarboxylic acid cycle 2 . Here we find that glucose-derived carbon is oxidized in mouse myocardium even when the MPC is genetically ablated. Using genetic and pharmacological tools, we demonstrate that lactate monocarboxylate transporter 1 (MCT1, encoded by Slc16a1 ) is required for the oxidation of glucose carbon by MPC-deficient myocardium. We further observe that MCT1, traditionally localized to the plasma membrane, also resides in the inner mitochondrial membrane of mouse and human cardiomyocytes. Together with matrix-localized LDHB, MCT1 enables mitochondrial lactate conversion to pyruvate and NADH, directly fueling the electron transport chain. Loss of MCT1 impairs lactate oxidation, disrupts metabolic flexibility and accelerates the development of heart failure with increased mortality after hyperactivation of the neurohormonal axis or ischemia–reperfusion injury. Thus, the existence of a parallel lactate-based pathway for carbohydrate oxidation can sustain cardiac energetics and maintain myocardial structure and function under diverse stress conditions.

item.title: T and B cells recognize splicing-derived neutrophil neoantigens in lupus
item.dc:creator: Rayan Najjar
Xiaoxing Wang
Farheen Shaikh
Ning Wang
Ethan Le
Jie An
Mohammad Pourshamsi
Cecilia Mustelin
item.description:
Authors: Rayan Najjar, Xiaoxing Wang, Farheen Shaikh, Ning Wang, Ethan Le, Jie An, Mohammad Pourshamsi, Cecilia Mustelin, et al.
Journal: Nature
Abstract: Abstract Proteome diversity is generated through alternative mRNA splicing 1 . In tumours, mis-spliced transcripts that contain intronic sequences, skipped exons or noncanonical donor/acceptor splice junctions resulting in frameshifts are often translated into neoantigens that drive anti-tumour immunity 2,3 . Here we report that neutrophils from patients with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), unlike neutrophils from healthy donors or patients with rheumatoid arthritis, contain many aberrantly spliced gene transcripts, the translation of which was predicted to result in novel amino acid sequences that are absent in normal splice variants or any other proteins. Twenty-one peptides derived from these novel amino acid sequences were detected by mass spectrometry on class I major histocompatibility complex molecules in patient samples. Co-culture of T cells from patients with overlapping sets of 15-mer peptides from the novel sequences resulted in the expansion of CD4 + and CD8 + T cells that were rapidly reactivated to secrete interferon-γ. T cell antigen receptor sequencing and re-expression transferred neoantigen reactivity to a reporter T cell. Serum from patients with SLE also contained IgG autoantibodies that recognized epitopes within the novel amino acid sequences. Our findings demonstrate that dysregulated mRNA splicing in SLE neutrophils generates neoantigens that have caused T and B cell activation, clonal expansion, IgG class-switch and autoimmunity.

item.title: Emotion regulation capacity lacks a shared neural signature
item.dc:creator: Maurizio Sicorello
Jenny Zaehringer
Thomas E. Kraynak
Peter J. Gianaros
Stephan Nebe
Lena M. Paschke
Rosa Steimke
Christine Stelzel
item.description:
Authors: Maurizio Sicorello, Jenny Zaehringer, Thomas E. Kraynak, Peter J. Gianaros, Stephan Nebe, Lena M. Paschke, Rosa Steimke, Christine Stelzel, et al.
Journal: Nature
Abstract: Abstract Cognitive reappraisal refers to changing how one thinks about a situation to alter its emotional impact. It is central to well-being 1 and engages prefrontal regulatory circuits 2 , prompting the assumption that their activity reflects a person’s capacity to regulate emotions 3–5 . Yet evidence for this assumption remains inconclusive and has not been established at scale. Here we analysed 40 task-based functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) datasets in a preregistered consortium with 2,175 participants and show that three widely used indicators of reappraisal capacity—trait questionnaires, task-based affective ratings and amygdala down-regulation—do not converge on a common core. Moreover, none of the three indicators showed the expected association with canonical prefrontal regulatory circuits. Trait questionnaires showed no detectable neural associations across the brain and task-based affective ratings were instead associated with responses in the amygdala and sensorimotor cortices. At the process level, canonical control circuits were engaged during both emotion generation and reappraisal, challenging their presumed specificity for emotion regulation. These findings caution against using activation in putatively regulatory brain regions to infer how well a person regulates emotions, with implications for neural biomarkers, interventions and psychoeducation that link emotion regulation difficulties to specific regional brain deficits.

item.title: Stone and water governed early human settlement of the desert
item.dc:creator: Rudolf W. Dellmour
Emily Coco
Osama Samawi
Mohammed Al Kindi
Ali Al Mahrooqi
Michelle R. Bebber
Metin I. Eren
Mathias Harzhauser
item.description:
Authors: Rudolf W. Dellmour, Emily Coco, Osama Samawi, Mohammed Al Kindi, Ali Al Mahrooqi, Michelle R. Bebber, Metin I. Eren, Mathias Harzhauser, et al.
Journal: Nature
Abstract: Abstract Models of early human dispersal rely on climate to predict where populations could settle, with freshwater assumed to govern the timing and geography 1,2 , particularly across the Saharo-Arabian arid belt, where humid windows episodically opened corridors into the desert interior 3 . Yet Pleistocene dispersals into ‘Green Arabia’ were brief and geographically constrained 4,5 , a pattern not explained by water availability alone. Here we show, from an approximately 1,500-km geoarchaeological survey through the Rub’ al Khali of Arabia, the largest sand sea in the world, that the availability of stone for tool manufacture operated as an independent factor on early human settlement. Palaeolake deposits were recorded at 55 of 125 localities investigated, yet no lithic artefacts and no knappable raw materials were found along the transect, with ground-surface visibility exceeding 95%, despite abundant freshwater and contemporary occupation at the desert margins. Spatial modelling of the Peninsula supports the inference that settlement tracked the co-occurrence of water and lithic raw materials rather than water alone. Across the Peninsula, 57% of water-accessible terrain lies on formations that lack knappable stone and adding raw-material availability raises discrimination of known site locations from an area under the curve of 0.695 to 0.768. Convergent patterns from Africa, North America and Asia indicate that the constraint is not peculiar to Arabia. Dispersal models that omit raw-material geology may systematically overestimate the habitable range of stone-tool-dependent populations.

item.title: Diet at disease onset determines tissue inflammatory memory
item.dc:creator: Zewen Jiang
John M. Tayeri
Im-Hong Sun
Joy Li
E. Dean Merrill
Longhui Qiu
Dongliang Zhang
Vrinda Johri
item.description:
Authors: Zewen Jiang, John M. Tayeri, Im-Hong Sun, Joy Li, E. Dean Merrill, Longhui Qiu, Dongliang Zhang, Vrinda Johri, et al.
Journal: Nature
Abstract: Abstract Obesity, which is often associated with prolonged exposure to an obesogenic diet, substantially alters immunity 1–7 , but whether brief dietary changes shape acute inflammatory responses and long-term tissue memory remains unclear. Here we show that transient high-fat diet (HFD) exposure at the onset of acute type 17 skin inflammation exacerbates disease in lean mice to levels comparable to those associated with chronic obesity. This effect is restricted to a discrete 4-day peri-initiation window; HFD outside this window has no impact, whereas switching obese mice to a low-fat diet (LFD) during a similar window fully blunts disease amplification. Mechanistically, HFD rapidly recruits neutrophils into the skin, and neutrophils in challenged skin express high levels of Nlrp3 (ref. 8 ) and Il1b . Neutrophil depletion, genetic Nlrp3 deficiency and pharmacological NLRP3 inhibition each blunt the HFD-induced inflammatory amplification. These findings nominate a neutrophil–NLRP3–IL-1β axis that licences pathogenic IL-1R1 + CD4 + T helper type 17 (T H 17) cells 9,10 . After recovery, a chromatin-poised tissue-resident memory T cell population persists. Consequently, mice exposed to HFD at disease onset develop exaggerated inflammation upon recurrence, despite recovery and maintenance on LFD. Transient HFD similarly amplifies lung T H 17 inflammation through neutrophil- and IL-1R1-dependent mechanisms. Together, these findings show that dietary state during a narrow temporal window can durably reprogram disease trajectory, suggesting that short-lived physiological states may become embedded in local immune memory 11 when they coincide with tissue inflammation.

item.title: Pharmacological inhibition of METTL1 as a therapy against solid and blood cancers
item.dc:creator: Eliza Yankova
Alexandra Sapetschnig
Beth Thomas
Siân Evans
Maria Eleftheriou
Malgorzata Gozdecka
Harry Fischl
Teresa Brevini
item.description:
Authors: Eliza Yankova, Alexandra Sapetschnig, Beth Thomas, Siân Evans, Maria Eleftheriou, Malgorzata Gozdecka, Harry Fischl, Teresa Brevini, et al.
Journal: Nature
Abstract: Abstract The N7-methylguanosine (m 7 G) modification is one of the most prevalent tRNA modifications, mainly catalysed by the METTL1–WDR4 protein complex 1–4 . The m 7 G methyltransferase METTL1 has been linked to oncogenic transformation and the maintenance of several aggressive malignancies; however, the clinical implications of therapeutically targeting a tRNA-modifying enzyme have not been established. Here we present the development and characterization of STM9005, a highly selective and potent first-in-class tRNA methyltransferase inhibitor of METTL1. Treatment of numerous cancer cell models (including leukaemia, melanoma, pancreatic carcinoma, oesophageal cancer and small cell lung carcinoma) with STM9005 blocks cell growth, causes differentiation changes and dysregulates cell cycle progression. These cellular effects were accompanied by a selective decrease in m 7 G on a subset of tRNAs and a reduction in their expression levels, which impacted the translation of oncogenic mRNAs. We show that pharmacological inhibition of METTL1 in vivo impairs tumour growth and significantly prolongs survival in multiple mouse cancer models of different tissue origin. Collectively, our results provide a strong proof of concept that targeting of tRNA methylation is a promising avenue of anti-cancer therapy and illustrate that catalytic inhibition of METTL1 represents a therapeutic strategy against a number of aggressive malignancies.
